# Asadisajātaka (Ja 181)

**ID:** Ja 181
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Asadisajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Prince Peerless
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja181

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Asadisajātaka* (Ja 181) is a birth story of the Pali Jātaka collection, situated as the opening narrative of the *Asadisavagga* in the second nipāta (*Dukanipāta*) [Fausböll 1879]. According to the frame story, the Buddha delivered this discourse while residing at Jetavana to illustrate the Great Renunciation (*mahābhinikkhamana*), declaring that his renunciation of kingship was not unique to his final life [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. In the story of the past set in Bārāṇasī during the reign of Brahmadatta, the Bodhisatta was born as Prince Asadisa ("Prince Peerless"), renowned for his skill in archery, while his younger brother was Prince Brahmadatta; at the age of sixteen, Asadisa travelled to Takkasilā to study under a world-renowned teacher [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. In the concluding identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the younger brother is identified as Ānanda and Prince Asadisa as the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1879].

The story found enduring resonance in the Theravāda literary tradition. According to the *Cūḷavaṃsa*, a king versed in Pali, Sanskrit, and grammar composed a poem in the Sinhala tongue (*Sīhala*) based on the *Asadisajātaka* [Geiger 1953], an adaptation reflected in later cataloged Sinhala literary works entitled *Asadisajātakaya* [Bendall 1893].

In terms of parallels and text reuse, SuttaCentral identifies a full Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit parallel in the *Mahāvastu* (Mvu 43: *The Jātaka of the Arrow that was Shot Far*) [SuttaCentral; Jones 1952]. DharmaNexus records four Pali-internal matching segments with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo), comprising 422 characters, with the longest shared segment (§0.4–2.4) exhibiting a similarity score of 0.94 [DharmaNexus].
